Culture
-------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Ostra_Aradalen1_Sweden.jpg/250px-Ostra_Aradalen1_Sweden.jpg)](./File:Ostra_Aradalen1_Sweden.jpg)

Traditional summer houses, *buvåll* "critter house" in Jämtland. 'Bu' is [cognate](./Cognate "Cognate") to the English word "booth" and 'våll' to "[weald](./Weald "Weald")"

[![Goats at Gräftåvallen, southern Jämtland](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Gr%C3%A4ft%C3%A5vallen.jpg/250px-Gr%C3%A4ft%C3%A5vallen.jpg)](./File:Gräftåvallen.jpg "Goats at Gräftåvallen, southern Jämtland")

Goats at Gräftåvallen, southern Jämtland

[![Jämthund](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/J%C3%A4mthund_drvd.png/250px-J%C3%A4mthund_drvd.png)](./File:Jämthund_drvd.png "Jämthund")

Jämthund

The culture of Jämtland has been greatly affected by the fact that Jämtland has never had an [upper class](./Upper_class "Upper class"), since the population have mostly consisted of free sovereign farmers with wide connections and a strong regional identity.[[26]](./Jämtland#cite_note-26) This has been the case for many generations. When [Christian IV of Denmark](./Christian_IV_of_Denmark "Christian IV of Denmark") punished the Jamts severely after having sworn the Swedish king their allegiance (see above) by turning them into [tenant farmers](./Tenant_farmer "Tenant farmer") and abolished their seal, he told them to stay put on their farms. They did not heed this call but instead sought help from their own organized advisors and "the land's defense", an insolence that further outraged the Danish king. Jämtland started out free and remained autonomous during its time as a Norwegian [dependency](./Dependent_territory "Dependent territory"). Because of Jämtland's historical background the local culture shows great similarities with the [Norwegian farm culture](./Norwegian_farm_culture "Norwegian farm culture").

Today, the history of Jämtland is exhibited in the regional museum [Jamtli](./Jamtli "Jamtli") in [Östersund](./Östersund "Östersund"). The museum consists of an [open-air section](./Open-air_museum "Open-air museum") with historical buildings, as well as an indoor museum which houses exhibitions about the region's cultural history, from the Stone Age until modern times. Local history has been very popular in Jämtland for over 100 years, due to the extensive cultural home ground movement that emerged in the late 19th and early 20th century. The movement founded Jamtli to preserve the cultural heritage.

### Lifestyle

The culture in Jämtland has been marked by the stages in human development; the hunting-gathering stage, the semi-nomadic herding stage, the fully agricultural stage and the modern technological stage.

Remnants from the hunter-gathering stage is first and foremost hunting itself. Jämtland's population remained in this stage for a very long time due to the hunters ability to sustain the population. Today the moose hunt is regarded by many Jamts as the major holiday of the year. When the first humans came to Jämtland they brought dogs with them as helpers. The local dog, [Jämthund](./Jämthund "Jämthund"), is a canine breed eponymous to Jämtland. Even if it is not explicitly stated, popular perception holds that the dog depicted in the coat of arms is of that breed. The Jämthund is often described having a [wolf](./Wolf "Wolf")-like appearance.

One of the first things [Tacitus](./Tacitus "Tacitus") mentions in his work *[Germania](./Germania_(book) "Germania (book)")* is that the Germanic people treasure their animals above all else. Tacitus also concludes that the Germanic people found cultivation repulsive. Instead, he states, the Germanic people devote themselves to food and sleep and besides that they prefer to remain idle. All of this, to certain extents, applied to Jämtland. When the people of Jämtland settled down they relied mostly on [pastoralism](./Pastoralism "Pastoralism") ([transhumance](./Transhumance "Transhumance")). Their animals were the source of wealth and they were therefore loved by their owners. This love for the [livestock](./Livestock "Livestock") has manifested itself in the dialect, a male [nipple](./Nipple "Nipple") is called *bokkjen* (the [buck](./Goat#Etymology "Goat")) and a female nipple is known as *geita* (the [goat](./Goat "Goat")).

In Jämtland the Scandinavian inland transhumance, *buföring*, has always been more important than cultivation. In fact it was crucial to take care of the livestock and supply them with food, and rewarding. Every summer for several weeks, from May to September, *gjetaran* (herd boys) and *butøusan* (herd girls, *bu* is cognate to "booth") followed and guarded *kreka*, the critter, on their way to a [grazing land](./Grazing "Grazing") on higher altitudes where several critter houses had been raised. The common animals taken out on these journeys were *gjettran* (Jämtland goats) and *kynnan* (the fell cows) a white, brisk and headstrong cow race, lacking horns. It was a hard work and it depended on cooperation between males and females. This lifestyle lived on for thousand years and it was first in the 1950s it became obsolete. This tradition has however been resurrected as of late, mostly for touristic purposes.

When the population settled down the society greatly changed, first coexisting with the older societies, later absorbing them. Trade became much more important, a political institution elected by the people came into existence, the very same institution whose successor is the current County Council. Jämtland got its name and a somewhat [hierarchical](./Hierarchy "Hierarchy") social structure emerged, though, as already pointed out, Jämtland never had an upper class. Strong families such as [Skanke](./Skanke "Skanke") and [Blix](./Blix_(noble_family)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Blix (noble family)") did exist though and on the countryside in Jämtland people still live in networks of relatives, *families*. Where they provide a second [social security](./Social_security "Social security") for many, in the rest of Sweden and in e.g. Östersund this has completely or almost entirely been replaced by [public welfare](./Public_welfare "Public welfare").

### Cuisine

See also: [Cuisine of Norway](./Cuisine_of_Norway "Cuisine of Norway") and [Cuisine of Sweden](./Cuisine_of_Sweden "Cuisine of Sweden")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Messmor.jpg/250px-Messmor.jpg)](./File:Messmor.jpg)

*Messmör*, soft whey butter, is a Jamtish product popular in Sweden

Much of Jämtland's cuisine is remnant from the herding stage. Just like other Scandinavians, it is common among Jamts to drink [milk](./Milk "Milk") throughout their entire life. There are many different types of Jamtish [dairy products](./Dairy_products "Dairy products"), especially cheese, since it was by far the easiest way to conserve milk. [Mesost](./Brunost "Brunost") is particularly associated with Jämtland and also e.g. a local variant of [cottage cheese](./Cottage_cheese "Cottage cheese") called *grynost*. In Jämtland there are several small [dairies](./Dairy "Dairy") in the villages, most famous is the one in [Skärvången](./Skärvången?action=edit&redlink=1 "Skärvången"). Other products associated with Jämtland are the [soft whey butter](./Soft_whey_butter?action=edit&redlink=1 "Soft whey butter"), [long fil](./Long_fil?action=edit&redlink=1 "Long fil"), [kjesfil](./Kjesfil?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kjesfil"), *flautgröt* "[cream](./Cream "Cream") [porridge](./Porridge "Porridge")", [tunnbröd](./Tunnbröd "Tunnbröd"), a version of [palt](./Palt "Palt") called *kams*, klobb etc.

The ancient practice of brewing *Julöl* (yule beer) persists even today with the [microbrewery](./Microbrewery "Microbrewery") [Jämtlands Bryggeri](./Jämtlands_Bryggeri "Jämtlands Bryggeri") in [Pilgrimstad](./Pilgrimstad "Pilgrimstad").

Local projects such as the internet portal [Food of Jämtland](http://www.foodofjamtland.se/english) and the trading mark *[Smakriket Jämtland](https://www.smakriket.se)* (the "taste realm" Jämtland) are two major contributors in marketing, preserving and developing the cuisine of Jämtland.

Some of the newest merchandises in Jämtland are a [sparkling wine](./Sparkling_wine "Sparkling wine") made of [birch](./Birch "Birch") [sap](./Sap "Sap") and a [sausage](./Sausage "Sausage") called *Jämtlandsfalu*, wilderness juice, the [snaps](./Snaps "Snaps") *kallsup* and tunnbröd [chips.](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/chips "wikt:chips")

### Folklore

See also: [Scandinavian folklore](./Scandinavian_folklore "Scandinavian folklore")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/PB190187.JPG/250px-PB190187.JPG)](./File:PB190187.JPG)

Lake Storsjön

The folklore of Jämtland mostly correspond to [Scandinavian folklore](./Scandinavian_folklore "Scandinavian folklore") as whole, although the folklore is seldom regarded as popular belief nowadays, with one major exception, [Storsjöodjuret](./Storsjöodjuret "Storsjöodjuret").

According to legend it is believed that [Storsjön](./Storsjön "Storsjön") (literally *the Great Lake*) harbors a large lake creature, Storsjöodjuret. There are many witness reports but the creature's existence remains to be established conclusively. Regardless of any proven existence, Storsjöodjuret was officially placed under the protection of a degree issued in 1986 by the [County Administrative Board](./County_Administrative_Boards_of_Sweden "County Administrative Boards of Sweden") to guarantee its safety from hunters and fortune seekers, the protection was lifted in November 2005.[[27]](./Jämtland#cite_note-27) The first description of Storsjöodjuret was made in this tale from 1635;

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg/250px-Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg)](./File:Draak_Östersund_22jul2006.jpg)

Storsjöodjuret is commonly represented by this figure.


> A long, long time ago two trolls, Jata and Kata, stood on the shores of the Great Lake brewing a concoction in their cauldrons. They brewed and mixed and added to the liquid for days and weeks and years. They knew not what would result from their brew but they wondered about it a great deal. One evening there was heard a strange sound from one of their cauldrons. There was a wailing, a groaning and a crying, then suddenly came a loud bang. A strange animal with a black serpentine body and a cat-like head jumped out of the cauldron and disappeared into the lake. The monster enjoyed living in the lake, grew unbelievably larger and awakened terror among the people whenever it appeared. Finally, it extended all the way round the island of Frösön, and could even bite its own tail. Ketil Runske bound the mighty monster with a strong spell which was carved on a stone and raised on the island of Frösön. The serpent was pictured on the stone. Thus was the spell to be tied till the day someone came who could read and understand the inscription on the stone.

*[Puken](./Puken?action=edit&redlink=1 "Puken")* is a magical ball of [yarn](./Yarn "Yarn") summoned by a witch to draw objects to her. It often steals milk to the witch by milking [cows](./Cow "Cow").[[28]](./Jämtland#cite_note-28)

Just like in the rest of the world [dragons](./Dragon "Dragon") have been known for a long time. In Jämtland they resemble [brooms](./Broom "Broom"), that flies quickly and strikes down where [treasuries](./Treasury "Treasury") are buried.[[29]](./Jämtland#cite_note-29)

*[Sjörå](./Sjörå "Sjörå")* is a keeper of freshwater, that master fish, [aas](./River "River") and lakes. It is similar to the Jamtish *[skogskjæringa](./Hulder "Hulder")* "wife of the forest". A being that, at day, takes the appearance of a *[rauvtjuksa](./Siberian_jay "Siberian jay")* "red tail", a bird seen as ominous in Jamtish folklore. When in physical form her tail is always apparent. She tries to lure men to have [sexual intercourse](./Sexual_intercourse "Sexual intercourse") with her. The *skogsrå* is not the same creature as skogskjæringa in Jamtish folklore, it is the keeper of the forest and master all the animals in it. It takes on the shape of a moose during hunting season, and grows larger and larger if hit by bullets and eventually forces the hunters out. It can however, be slain with a silver bullet.[[30]](./Jämtland#cite_note-30)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Johan_Tirens_naecken.jpg/250px-Johan_Tirens_naecken.jpg)](./File:Johan_Tirens_naecken.jpg)

Local artist [Johan Tirén](./Johan_Tirén "Johan Tirén")'s painting *Jämtlandssägen* (Jämtland's tale) with a young fiddler wearing traditional Great Jamtish clothes, whilst listening to the Nix play.

[Tomten](./Tomte "Tomte") is a common creature, it is quite tall and has an eye in the middle of his forehead. It is the keeper of [barns](./Barn "Barn") and a very capricious being, though he usually brings luck.[[31]](./Jämtland#cite_note-p_98-31)

The [Nix](./Neck_(water_spirit) "Neck (water spirit)"), *Näkkjen*, is a common mythical creature, in Jämtland it refers to a male water spirit whose music was dangerous to women. Each year in the town of [Hackås](./Hackås "Hackås") in southern Jämtland an annual [traditional music](./Traditional_Nordic_dance_music "Traditional Nordic dance music") contest *[Årets Näck](./Årets_Näck "Årets Näck")* is held where each contestant impersonates the Nix.

In Jämtland the [vættir](./Vættir "Vættir")/[dwarves](./Dwarf_(mythology) "Dwarf (mythology)") goes by the name *jolbyggar* "earth builders". They herd large white goats and cows and live underground, they are considered innocuous though sometimes they exchange an unbaptized child for a so-called *bytningsbarn*. They are commonly associated with the grazing lands.[[31]](./Jämtland#cite_note-p_98-31) They also go by the names *småruskan*, *smågubban* and *småtussan*.

### Folk costumes

Jämtland has several different types of folk costumes or *[bunads](./Bunad "Bunad")*. Unlike certain regions in Scandinavia a unitary bunad did not exist in Jämtland's parishes, with the exception of [Hammerdal parish](./Hammerdal_parish?action=edit&redlink=1 "Hammerdal parish") with its [brown](./Brown "Brown")-striped clothing.

Usually Jämtland is divided into three different clothing parts, the North Jamtish ([Hammerdal](./Hammerdal_Court_District "Hammerdal Court District")), the East Jamtish ([Ragunda](./Ragunda_Court_District "Ragunda Court District")) and the Great Jamtish area, covering the rest and the majority of Jämtland.

The North Jamtish clothing part is typically influenced by the folk costumes of northern Ångermanland and to a lesser degree Lapland, with the exception of [Frostviken parish](./Frostviken_parish?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frostviken parish") settled by [Trønders](./Trøndersk "Trøndersk") in the 18th century. The East Jamtish part is the least old-fashioned of the three with many changes done to the costumes through time, making them closer to the kind used at the Swedish coast, rather than the others in Jämtland. The Great Jamtish part has typically old-fashioned and conservative homogeneous bunads with blue socks, red knitted caps among the males, dark bounded caps for ladies and coloured for girls. The skirts are usually of a single colour and the men have blue or black [hodden](./Hodden "Hodden") [coats](./Coat_(clothing) "Coat (clothing)"), with yellow [chamois leather](./Chamois_leather "Chamois leather") pants made from moose skin.

### Dialects

The genuine dialect of Jämtland is [Jamtish](./Jamtish "Jamtish"). The speakers of the dialect refer to it as *Jamska* ([ˈjamskɐ]), which is a definite form that translates to English as "the Jamtish". However, due to the lack of a well-established English name of the dialect both Jamtish and Jamtlandic are used.

Jamtish is in fact a group of dialects and there are distinctive dialects in every parish. Though they are usually classified in four groups; *framlänningsmålet* "the Central Jamtish tongue", *opplänningsmålet* (spoken in Western Jämtland), Southwest Jamtish and Northern Jamtish. The dialects in eastern Jämtland are sometimes considered as a fifth group of Jamtish, but also as dialects more related to the Swedish dialects spoken in [Ångermanland](./Ångermanland "Ångermanland"). In the very north of Jämtland *lidmål*, a version of [Trøndersk](./Trøndersk "Trøndersk"), is spoken. Jamtish is spoken by 50 000 people at most living in Jämtland and in other areas of Sweden, particularly the capital [Stockholm](./Stockholm "Stockholm").

### Language

Even if the Jamtish official status is a dialect many Jamtish people see it as an own language. There are multiple activists that are trying to make the Swedish government recognise Jamtish as a minority language just as [Yiddish](./Yiddish "Yiddish") or [Sami](./Sami_people "Sami people") have become one. The claimers say to look at the different words and pronunciations of them. Whether or not it is its own language has been widely debated since the early 20th century.

### Provincial character

Historically each province in Sweden has been known for a specific provincial character or *[volksgeist](./Volksgeist "Volksgeist")*. This was a field of intense research in Sweden earlier but is viewed somewhat unmodern and considered prejudice today.

The provincial character of Jämtland was often portrayed as cheerful and the population have historically been known for their hospitality. Before the dawn of the railway it was common among farmers to leave their doors unlocked when the annual summer journey to the critter houses was due, often with the table set with food for travelers.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Ostersund.JPG/250px-Ostersund.JPG)](./File:Ostersund.JPG)

Östersund was founded to stop the faring traditions in Jämtland. This happened first after the railroad was established and the city is now the trading center of Jämtland.

The faring traditions of Jämtland are also very characteristic. The Jamts were known to neglect the agriculture and instead take on long trading journeys all over Scandinavia to various [markets](./Market_(place) "Market (place)") such as the ancients ones in [Levanger](./Levanger_(town) "Levanger (town)") and [Gregorius market](./Gregorius_market?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gregorius market") on Frösön. This was regarded as sheer pleasure in itself and not as something they were obligated to do. In the middle of the 18th century Jämtland's population was roughly 20 000 and it was common that over 1 000 Jamts were present during *Marsimartnan* in Levanger, it is also claimed that the city was built solely on spikes from Jämtland before the fire in the 19th century. The journeys took place during the winters when the landscape was more accessible (when [swamps](./Swamp "Swamp"), lakes and [tarns](./Tarn_(lake) "Tarn (lake)") froze to ice) and was conducted by males, which left the females in complete charge of the [household](./Household "Household") and the [property](./Property "Property"). The journeys were well-organized [expeditions](./Exploration "Exploration") and no one traveled alone. These traditions has awarded the Jamt with traits such as enterprising and energetic. The Jamts' attempts to avoid tariffs were very successful which greatly angered Swedish officials through time. These journeys eventually stopped once the railway came, though it has recently been renewed by locals. Some say that the heritage from this age lives on, given the high number of enterprises per capita.

### Republic of Jamtland

Main article: [Republic of Jamtland](./Republic_of_Jamtland "Republic of Jamtland")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg/250px-Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg.png)](./File:Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg)

[Flag of the Republic of Jamtland](./Flag_of_the_Republic_of_Jamtland "Flag of the Republic of Jamtland")

In the 1960s, an [independence movement](./Independence_movement "Independence movement") calling itself the "Republic of Jamtland" was created by humorist/actor/director [Yngve Gamlin](./Yngve_Gamlin "Yngve Gamlin"). Motivated on paper as an attempt to return the province to Jamtlandic control, the republic was given some form of recognition in 1967 when Mr. Gamlin was invited to an event for visiting statesmen hosted by Swedish prime minister [Tage Erlander](./Tage_Erlander "Tage Erlander"). Described in some sources as a form of criticism against [centralized](./Centralized "Centralized") Swedish government and in others as a [marketing](./Marketing "Marketing") ploy, it is likely that both played some part in its foundation (Republic officials typically describe it as "51 percent serious"). The republic has a self-styled [flag](./Flag_of_the_Republic_of_Jamtland "Flag of the Republic of Jamtland") and national anthem ([Jämtlandssången](./Jämtlandssången "Jämtlandssången")) and the independence movement hosts the annual [Storsjöyran](./Storsjöyran "Storsjöyran") event in the capital, [Östersund](./Östersund "Östersund").

### Sports

Football in the province is administered by [Jämtland-Härjedalens Fotbollförbund](./Jämtland-Härjedalens_Fotbollförbund "Jämtland-Härjedalens Fotbollförbund"). The clubs overseen by the association include [Myssjö-Ovikens IF](./Myssjö-Ovikens_IF "Myssjö-Ovikens IF").

**Bräcke Municipality** ([Swedish](./Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Bräcke kommun*) is a [municipality](./Municipalities_of_Sweden "Municipalities of Sweden") in [Jämtland County](./Jämtland_County "Jämtland County") in northern [Sweden](./Sweden "Sweden"). Its [seat](./Administrative_centre "Administrative centre") is located in [Bräcke](./Bräcke "Bräcke").

The present municipality was formed in 1974 when "old" Bräcke Municipality was amalgamated with Kälarne and Revsund. The three former municipalities had been created in 1952. The number of original entities (as of 1863) were six. Due to the declining population in the area further amalgamations have been proposed, but rejected.

**Östersund** (pronounced [[œstɛˈʂɵnːd]](./Help:IPA/Swedish "Help:IPA/Swedish") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Sv-%C3%96stersund.ogg "File:Sv-Östersund.ogg"); [Southern Sami](./Southern_Sami_language "Southern Sami language"): *Staare*) is an [urban area](./Urban_areas_in_Sweden "Urban areas in Sweden") ([city](./Stad_(Sweden) "Stad (Sweden)")) in [Jämtland](./Jämtland "Jämtland") in northern Sweden. It is the seat of [Östersund Municipality](./Östersund_Municipality "Östersund Municipality") and the capital of [Jämtland County](./Jämtland_County "Jämtland County"). Östersund is located at the shores of Sweden's fifth-largest lake, [Storsjön](./Storsjön "Storsjön"), opposite the island [Frösön](./Frösön "Frösön"). It is the only city in Jämtland. The northern part of the urban area is located inside of the municipality of [Krokom](./Krokom_Municipality "Krokom Municipality").

Östersund is the region's cultural and economical centre and by tradition a city of trade and commerce. The city had one of the most extensive [garrisons](./Garrison "Garrison") in Sweden prior to its closure in the early-21st century. Östersund is home to [Mid Sweden University](./Mid_Sweden_University "Mid Sweden University")'s largest campus site with approximately 7,000 students. With a total population of 50,960 (2017) Östersund is the [22nd most populous city in Sweden](./List_of_cities_in_Sweden_by_population "List of cities in Sweden by population"), the [46th most populous city in Scandinavia](./List_of_cities_in_Scandinavia_by_population "List of cities in Scandinavia by population"), and by far the largest inland city in [Northern Sweden](./Norrland "Norrland").

The city was the only Swedish city founded and chartered in the 18th century. Östersund was founded in order to create a trade monopoly over Jämtland whose inhabitants' lucrative trade annoyed the Swedish Crown. The intention was to persuade the local farmers to deliver merchandise to middlemen in Östersund, but the population opposed this economic philosophy, and Östersund long remained small.[[5]](./Östersund#cite_note-found-5) It took until the end of the 19th century for Östersund to truly become a city, after the arrival of the railroad and the [economic liberalization](./Economic_liberalization "Economic liberalization") of that time.

Östersund is situated in inland Scandinavia and connected to [Sundsvall](./Sundsvall "Sundsvall") in the east on the Swedish coast, and [Trondheim](./Trondheim "Trondheim") in the west at the shores of the [Norwegian Sea](./Norwegian_Sea "Norwegian Sea"). Östersund is located in the middle of [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia "Scandinavia"), in the middle of Sweden, in the middle of Jämtland County and in the middle of Östersund Municipality. As the most centrally located city in Sweden, the city credits itself as the *[centre of Sweden](./Geographical_center_of_Sweden "Geographical center of Sweden")*.[[6]](./Östersund#cite_note-6)[[7]](./Östersund#cite_note-7)

Östersund is marketed as *Vinterstaden* – Winter City.[[8]](./Östersund#cite_note-8)[[9]](./Östersund#cite_note-9) Winter City as a project is run by the municipality together with city enterprises. While winters are long, the [local climate](./Östersund#Climate) is only moderately cold by elevated and northerly Swedish standards, but with chilly summers. Östersund has had a long history as a centre of outdoor activities with a modern [cross-country ski](./Cross-country_skiing_(sport) "Cross-country skiing (sport)") stadium and an actual [piste](./Piste "Piste") in the city itself. Östersund has also hosted several [World Championships](./World_Championships "World Championships") in various sports such as [biathlon](./Biathlon "Biathlon"), [speed skating](./Speed_skating "Speed skating") and [ski orienteering](./Orienteering#Ski_orienteering "Orienteering") along with Swedish National Championships in cross-country skiing and [snocross](./Snocross "Snocross"). The city has been the applicant city of Sweden for several [Winter Olympic Games](./Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"), but has yet to host one. The precursor to the Winter Olympic Games, the *[Nordic Games](./Nordic_Games "Nordic Games")*, were however held at several occasions in the city, due to lack of snow in [Stockholm](./Stockholm "Stockholm").[[10]](./Östersund#cite_note-10)

Geography
---------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6n_and_%C3%96stersund_WorldWind.jpg/250px-Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6n_and_%C3%96stersund_WorldWind.jpg)](./File:Frösön_and_Östersund_WorldWind.jpg)

Satellite image of Östersund and the island of [Frösön](./Frösön "Frösön").

Östersund is the only city in the province and is located on the shore of [Storsjön](./Storsjön "Storsjön"), the fifth largest lake in Sweden. The area surrounding this lake is commonly referred to as [Storsjöbygden](./Storsjöbygden?action=edit&redlink=1 "Storsjöbygden") and has been described as the world's northernmost located genuine agricultural society in the inland with [continental climate](./Continental_climate "Continental climate").[[11]](./Östersund#cite_note-11)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/%C3%96stersund_from_Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6n.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersund_from_Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6n.jpg)](./File:Östersund_from_Frösön.jpg)

Östersund and Frösön in February 2005

The city sprawls along the eastern slopes of lake Storsjön with most of the city, and the city core itself, located on the mainland, facing the non mainland part of the city, the island of [Frösön](./Frösön "Frösön"), which for a very long time was the actual centre of Jämtland. Today, a sizeable part of the city's population live on the slopes of the island that face the city centre. Östersund is a bimunicipal town because a minor part of it, with roughly 400 inhabitants, is actually situated in [Krokom Municipality](./Krokom_Municipality "Krokom Municipality").

The city spans across *Östersundet* and the city was named after this strait. Östersund can be directly translated from Swedish to English as "East [Sound](./Sound_(geography) "Sound (geography)")". The name of the strait derives from an older [Jamtish](./Jamtlandic "Jamtlandic") name now present in the form *Åstersånn*.

### Climate

Östersund has a [subarctic climate](./Subarctic_climate "Subarctic climate") ([Köppen](./Köppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): Dfc) and is located in the far north of the north temperate climate zone. The cold [Arctic](./Arctic "Arctic") winds that occasionally find their way to the city are called *nordvästan* ('the north-westerner') or *kallvästan* ('the cold-westerner') locally.[[12]](./Östersund#cite_note-12)

The winter climate is much warmer than most locations at similar latitudes. This is due to the [Gulf Stream](./Gulf_Stream "Gulf Stream") and the many passages in the mountain range, bringing warmer [Atlantic](./Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") winds to the city during winters. This somewhat [maritime](./Maritime_climate "Maritime climate") character also makes the summers in the city rather cool, in comparison to other towns in inland Scandinavia, which all have a more continental climate with cold winters and warm summers.[[13]](./Östersund#cite_note-clim-13) It contains a strong influence of the [humid continental climate](./Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") (Dfb) courtesy of its mild September lows extending the mild mean temperatures.

Though Östersund is in fact affected by the Gulf Stream, it lacks the high frequency of rain or snow following the currents. This is due to the Scandinavian Mountain Range acting as a natural barrier, receiving most of the [precipitation](./Precipitation_(meteorology) "Precipitation (meteorology)"), giving Östersund and the surrounding area a rain deficit.[[13]](./Östersund#cite_note-clim-13) Another issue that has to be taken into account is the higher elevation of Östersund compared to the weather stations in [Ångermanland](./Ångermanland "Ångermanland") farther east. For example, [Sollefteå](./Sollefteå "Sollefteå") at a similar latitude 130 kilometres (81 mi) to the east but near sea level in an inland valley, has three degrees warmer July days. There is often [temperature inversion](./Inversion_(meteorology) "Inversion (meteorology)") between Östersund and lower areas in winter.

Östersund has a high exposition of sunlight and was the sunniest city in Sweden in the summer of 2007 (1 July to 9 August) with 654 hours of sun.[[14]](./Östersund#cite_note-14) However, in comparison to east coast locations, sunshine is relatively low.

Cityscape
---------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg/250px-Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg)](./File:Draak_Östersund_22jul2006.jpg)

[Storsjöodjuret](./Storsjöodjuret "Storsjöodjuret") (the Great lake monster) is a [cryptid](./Cryptid "Cryptid") said to inhabit lake [Storsjön](./Storsjön "Storsjön"). This figure has often been used as a symbol for Östersund, along with the moose (see above).

Östersund was laid out with roads spanning from north to south countered by several [alleys](./Alley "Alley") from east to west, which is why an alley in Östersund is synonymous with a road leading down towards Storsjön. From the inner city one may gaze upon Storsjön, Frösön and the Jamtish [fell](./Fell "Fell") region with snow-clad mountains. This was made possible due to the [topography](./Topography "Topography") and the [grid plan](./Grid_plan "Grid plan").

The regularity in Östersund's road system and the slanting alleys leading from higher altitudes down towards Storsjön have created the "windows to the west" characteristic and unique to Östersund as a city.[[17]](./Östersund#cite_note-17) The alleys, often seen as rather steep, have created the illusion that the houses in the city core are climbing to higher grounds. These houses were conformed upon their construction to fit with the slopes.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/%C3%96stersund_badhusparken.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersund_badhusparken.jpg)](./File:Östersund_badhusparken.jpg)

Badhusparken

The first city plan of Östersund was made with several large segments in the core being reserved as [green areas](./Green "Green"). Östersund was thus planned as a green city and special lots, e.g. *kryddgårdstomter* 'spice garden lots' were created along with construction lots. These lots shifted with a construction lot alternating with a spice garden lot. The garden lots are no longer existent since they too have been constructed upon. Many of the fences that separated each lot from another with trees and verdure were left intact. The large green areas are still present, with parks such as Kyrkparken, Österängsparken and Badhusparken being the most prominent. Badhusparken was once the location of a large [bath house](./Public_bathing "Public bathing") (hence the name *Badhus*-) though it was torn down in 1881 when the railway was constructed. A new larger two-storey pompous bath house was later built on poles a few metres from the shore, enabling the population to bathe in the waters of Storsjön during summers. This house was also torn down when a new bath house with heated water was founded in 1938.[[18]](./Östersund#cite_note-18)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/%C3%96stersund_winter_festival.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersund_winter_festival.jpg)](./File:Östersund_winter_festival.jpg)

The national romantic Sparbanken building illuminated during the Winter Festival.

When Östersund started to grow as a city in the late 19th century the houses consisted predominantly of wood, though stone had become popular in the central parts. These houses were heavily characterized by [Neo-Gothicism](./Gothic_Revival_architecture "Gothic Revival architecture") and [Neo-Renaissance](./Neo-Renaissance "Neo-Renaissance") architecture.[[19]](./Östersund#cite_note-19) A very common feature of these houses were [towers](./Tower "Tower"), some even resembling those on old castles like the one on [Hotell Grand](./Hotell_Grand?action=edit&redlink=1 "Hotell Grand") at the main square. In the early 20th century a new age had come and in the main road, Prästgatan, the new age came fiercely. The wooden houses were replaced by stone buildings, because a city's well-being was measured in how many stone buildings it had. At the same time [military barracks](./Military_barracks "Military barracks") were constructed in connection to the older settlement.[[20]](./Östersund#cite_note-20) [Jugendstil](./Jugendstil "Jugendstil") became popular too as an addition to the [National Romantic style](./National_Romantic_style "National Romantic style") architecture.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Storgatan_in_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Storgatan_in_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Storgatan_in_Östersund.jpg)

Storgatan in Östersund with an alley, a window to the west, down towards the Storsjön lake.

In the 1930s, the [functionalistic style](./Functionalism_(architecture) "Functionalism (architecture)") made itself apparent in Östersund's outskirts, which were growing. In the 1940s, the city was made more car-friendly and the city was first and foremost planned for cars.[[21]](./Östersund#cite_note-21) Later sanitation issues were brought up, which resulted in the construction of a [sewage treatment works](./Sewage_treatment_works "Sewage treatment works") and waste water was no longer flushed directly into Storsjön. Östersund was also affected by the [Million Programme](./Million_Programme "Million Programme"), though to a lesser extent than other cities. During the same period older buildings such as Hotell Grand (to make room for Storsjöteatern), Cellfängelset (a jail located at the beginning of Prästgatan), Flickskolan (the girl school next to the city hall, where the current county library is located) and Västra stationen (at Badhusparken) were torn down. The local media described it as "demolishing madness".[[22]](./Östersund#cite_note-22) When the Good Templar house was threatened in order to widen Rådhusgatan the city's inhabitants had had enough and the building was saved.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Storgatan_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Storgatan_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Storgatan_Östersund.jpg)

Storgatan with a "spice garden lot" to the left.

The buildings along Storgatan (literally: 'the large street') with entire segments intact since the 1880s are considered one of the best preserved city settlements in Sweden. The wooden façades are rich with details and the house are relatively low, short and slim. A great amount of work was put down on creating a balance between details and entirety. Parallel with Storgatan lies Prästgatan – 'the priest street', Östersund's main shopping street. The buildings between the two streets are often connected and the streets create small rooms mostly inaccessible for keen winds. These so-called rooms also stimulate the social life on the streets.[*[clarification needed](./Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*]

Stortorget – the main [town square](./Town_square "Town square") in central Östersund is one of six "closed squares" built in Sweden, the others being the ones in [Uppsala](./Uppsala "Uppsala"), [Karlstad](./Karlstad "Karlstad"), [Vimmerby](./Vimmerby "Vimmerby"), [Piteå](./Piteå "Piteå") and [Haparanda](./Haparanda "Haparanda"). It was created through indentation in four different blocks to deliberately create an open air room with openings to every direction, a style deriving from how cities were planned during [the Renaissance](./The_Renaissance "The Renaissance"). However the town square lost its original shape when it was opened up and expanded towards the lake. Stortorget has long been the city's main market place and core; it is also here that the thousand-year-old market *[Gregorie market](./Gregorie_market?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gregorie market")* is held each year in March. The city festival *[Storsjöyran](./Storsjöyran "Storsjöyran")* has Stortorget as its main centre.

### Districts and housing estates

Before Östersund was established the population in the area was very scarce. In [Odensala](./Odensala?action=edit&redlink=1 "Odensala") and [Torvalla](./Torvalla "Torvalla") older settlements existed; the name Odensala can be derived from the Viking age and the Halls of [Odin](./Odin "Odin") (though Torvalla means 'dry wealds' with no reference to [Thor](./Thor "Thor")). These two villages were later incorporated into Östersund and are today two major urban districts. Besides them the urban districts of [Staden](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staden,%20Östersund "sv:Staden, Östersund"), [Norr](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norr,%20Östersund "sv:Norr, Östersund"), [Söder](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Söder,%20Östersund "sv:Söder, Östersund"), [Odenslund](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odenslund "sv:Odenslund"), [Karlslund](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlslund,%20Östersund "sv:Karlslund, Östersund"), [Körfältet](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Körfältet "sv:Körfältet"), [Odenskog](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odenskog "sv:Odenskog"), [Lugnvik](./Lugnvik "Lugnvik") are found on the mainland of Östersund. On the island Frösön are the six urban districts [Hornsberg](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornsberg,%20Östersund "sv:Hornsberg, Östersund"), [Östberget](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Östberget "sv:Östberget"), [Frösödal](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frösödal "sv:Frösödal"), [Mjälle](./Mjälle?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mjälle"), [Valla](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valla,%20Östersund "sv:Valla, Östersund") and [Härke](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Härke "sv:Härke").

The central parts of Östersund are a part of the urban district *[Staden](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staden,%20Östersund "sv:Staden, Östersund")* – 'the city', which has become synonymous with Östersund for many people living in the nearby villages and towns. As Östersund is the only city in the area and nearest city for many it is common to call it *Stan*, though the [dative form](./Dative_case "Dative case") *Staa* has increasingly grown unusual. The residents of Östersund are referred to as *östersundare*, though local people in rural areas call them *stassbon* 'towners', and *stassbo* 'towner', in [singular](./Grammatical_number "Grammatical number").

### Landmarks

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Ostersund_city_hall.jpg/250px-Ostersund_city_hall.jpg)](./File:Ostersund_city_hall.jpg)

Östersund City Hall

The most well-known landmark of Östersund is the national romantic [Östersund City Hall](./Östersund_City_Hall?action=edit&redlink=1 "Östersund City Hall") [[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Östersunds%20rådhus "sv:Östersunds rådhus")] (*Östersunds rådhus*). It is 51 meters tall, contains 136 rooms and opened in 1912. It is the greatest constructional symbol of the National Romantic architecture in Östersund.[[23]](./Östersund#cite_note-23) The city hall looks almost like a fortress and has a particular connection to the local art of Jämtland. The [bell tower](./Bell_tower "Bell tower") is of typical Jamtish design, shaped like an [onion](./Onion_dome "Onion dome"). Local sculptor [Olof Ahlberg](./Olof_Ahlberg "Olof Ahlberg") (1876–1956) made most of the sculptural details and the ornaments are made from Jamtish [limestone](./Limestone "Limestone").[[24]](./Östersund#cite_note-24)

Östersund City Hall was designed by [Frans Bertil Wallberg](./Frans_Bertil_Wallberg?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frans Bertil Wallberg") [[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frans%20Bertil%20Wallberg "sv:Frans Bertil Wallberg")] (1862–1935) and was seen by contemporary colleagues as the best of modern Swedish architecture.[[25]](./Östersund#cite_note-25) The main part of the building is accentuated by a grand tower and a monumental stairway. It is accompanied by only one wing, the north wing, as the second, south wing, was torn down in the 1970s.[[26]](./Östersund#cite_note-26)[*[failed verification](./Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*]

A recently built landmark is *Arctura*, named after Jämtland's provincial star [Arcturus](./Arcturus "Arcturus"), a large hot water accumulator tank. Due to its appearance it is referred to as *Termosen* ('the [Thermos](./Vacuum_flask "Vacuum flask")'). At night the 65-meter building is illuminated with various lights to give the appearance of sunrise and the [Aurora Borealis](./Aurora_(astronomy) "Aurora (astronomy)"), for example.

History
-------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6stenen.jpg/250px-Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6stenen.jpg)](./File:Frösöstenen.jpg)

The Frösö Runestone is situated on Frösön in Östersund.



Main article: [History of Östersund](./History_of_Östersund "History of Östersund")

Lake Storsjön's shores have long been inhabited. The area where Östersund is situated was for a very long time Frösön's link to the east mainland. Frösön, the island of the [Norse god](./Norse_god "Norse god") [Freyr](./Freyr "Freyr"), was originally the centre of the region and it was here the only inland Scandinavian [hill fort](./Hill_fort "Hill fort"), [Mjälleborgen](./Mjälleborgen?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mjälleborgen"), was built around 300 AD. The ancient [Scandinavian thing](./Thing_(assembly) "Thing (assembly)") [Jamtamót](./Jamtamót "Jamtamót") was held on this island, the christening of Jämtland begun here and it was here the world's northernmost raised runestone, [Frösö Runestone](./Frösö_Runestone "Frösö Runestone"), was raised.

Plans regarding the foundation of a [Swedish city](./Stad_(Sweden) "Stad (Sweden)") or *[köping](./Köping "Köping")* (market town, 'Chipping') in Jämtland existed among governmental officials already after the previously Norwegian province was ceded from [Denmark-Norway](./Denmark-Norway "Denmark-Norway") in 1645. [Queen Christina](./Christina_of_Sweden "Christina of Sweden") demanded the establishment of a [sconce](./Sconce_(fortification) "Sconce (fortification)") on [Andersön](./Andersön?action=edit&redlink=1 "Andersön") shortly after the province became Swedish; this sconce would together with [Frösö sconce](./Frösö_sconce?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frösö sconce") secure Swedish control of Jämtland.[[27]](./Östersund#cite_note-27) Christina's intention was to locate the "Jamts' city" within this [fortification](./Fortification "Fortification"). In order to construct the sconce the local inhabitants were coerced into [forced labour](./Forced_labour "Forced labour") 1651 but after protests and lack of [capital](./Capital_(economics) "Capital (economics)") the project was ended in 1654.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Old_%C3%96stersund.png/250px-Old_%C3%96stersund.png)](./File:Old_Östersund.png)

Östersund in the mid-19th century, the church in the picture was the first church in Östersund. When the houses were smaller it dominated the cityscape.

In 1758, the plans were brought back up through an initiative from the chief financial director [Pehr Schissler](./Pehr_Schissler?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pehr Schissler") and the proposition did however initiate a new debate whether or not a city was to be established in Jämtland, in order to counteract the trading and [faring traditions](./Jämtland#Provincial_character "Jämtland") of Jämtland's farmers.[[5]](./Östersund#cite_note-found-5) Several other attempts at concentration had previously been taken, and deemed unsatisfactory.[[28]](./Östersund#cite_note-28) Östersund was founded and given its charter by Monarch [Gustav III of Sweden](./Gustav_III_of_Sweden "Gustav III of Sweden") on 23 October 1786, shortly after the outskirt of the Odensala farmers' lands were bought for the purpose. Several other places had been suggested, like [Huså](./Huså?action=edit&redlink=1 "Huså"), the then-largest settlement in Jämtland, along with [Krokom](./Krokom "Krokom"), [Sunne](./Sunne_(Jämtland)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sunne (Jämtland)") and Ede outside of [Brunflo](./Brunflo "Brunflo"). Frösön was also a candidate but the lot fell on Östersund, as it was deemed most favourable.[[5]](./Östersund#cite_note-found-5) The only things actually located in the area at the time were the main road and the bridge to Frösön. Östersund was upon its foundation freed from taxes for a period of 20 years and completely liberated from trade regulations and [guild](./Guild "Guild") order.[[5]](./Östersund#cite_note-found-5) In other remote locations of the [Nordic region](./Nordic_region "Nordic region"), similar cities were founded, like [Reykjavík](./Reykjavík "Reykjavík") in Iceland the very same year, [Tromsø](./Tromsø "Tromsø") (1794) in [Northern Norway](./Northern_Norway "Northern Norway") and [Tampere](./Tampere "Tampere") (1775) and [Kuopio](./Kuopio "Kuopio") (1782) in the Finnish [inland](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/inland "wikt:inland"). Östersund is however the only city in present-day Sweden to have been founded in the 18th century.[[29]](./Östersund#cite_note-29)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/%C3%96stersunds_centralstation_01.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersunds_centralstation_01.jpg)](./File:Östersunds_centralstation_01.jpg)

The main railway station was built in 1879

The city developed poorly and had to struggle in its infancy.[[30]](./Östersund#cite_note-30) The state tried to persuade the Jamtish traders on Frösön to migrate to the new city but they had no intentions of leaving such a rich parish with the fertile soils Frösön consisted of in favour of the swamp and marshes across the strait. During its first 50 years the city's population only grew by an average of eight people per year.[[31]](./Östersund#cite_note-Rum-31) The city became the county seat of the newly founded county consisting of the provinces Jämtland and [Härjedalen](./Härjedalen "Härjedalen") in 1810, and a county council was established.[[31]](./Östersund#cite_note-Rum-31) Though, Östersund remained a de facto farming village with fewer than 400 inhabitants in 1820.[[32]](./Östersund#cite_note-32) An upswing occurred in the 1850s, as trade was liberalized and the logging industry developed.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/%C3%96stersund%2C_gamla_teatern.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersund%2C_gamla_teatern.jpg)](./File:Östersund,_gamla_teatern.jpg)

"The Old Theatre", originally built as an [IOGT](./IOGT "IOGT") assembly house in 1884. Now a hotel and a restaurant.

It took until the construction of the railroad in 1879 before Östersund became a real city and actually gained the status as Jämtland's centre, at Frösön's expense. Thanks to the "farmer chieftain" [Nils Larson i Tullus](./Nils_Larson_i_Tullus?action=edit&redlink=1 "Nils Larson i Tullus"), the railroad came to pass through the city itself instead of outside it, as planned. The railway from coast to coast across the then-union between [Sweden and Norway](./Sweden_and_Norway "Sweden and Norway") was finished in 1882, connecting Östersund more closely to [Trondheim](./Trondheim "Trondheim") and Sundsvall. Östersund then came to grow faster than any other Swedish city. After ten years it had passed 20 Swedish cities in population.[[33]](./Östersund#cite_note-33) The city attracted immigrants, a slight majority from the Jamtish countryside, though still with a high number of settlers from southern Sweden.[[34]](./Östersund#cite_note-34) While Östersund was in its most intense state of growth, [popular movements](./Social_movement "Social movement") emerged among the inhabitants. In Jämtland and Härjedalen the [Good Templar movement](./IOGT "IOGT") (a part of the [temperance movement](./Temperance_movement "Temperance movement")) came to dominate completely. In 1883, 700 of the city's total population of 3,000 were organized Good Templars. The greatest symbol of the movements grandeur was the Order House constructed in 1885 in the city, *Östersunds-Goodtemplars-Ordenshus*. When one of the most prominent leaders, [Joseph Malins](./Joseph_Malins "Joseph Malins"), visited the city he announced that it was the world's largest order house.[[35]](./Östersund#cite_note-35)

Many of the leading people behind the popular movements in Östersund saw industrialization as a significant threat to the native districts and the old village and farming community. The work from the movements made the city and its centre-right governance extremely hostile to industry. Instead they wanted to portray Östersund as a centre of [outdoor activities](./Outdoor_activity "Outdoor activity"), culture, education and tourism. Industry was not allowed to threaten the good environment and [cultural history](./Cultural_history "Cultural history") traditions.

In 1917 when the [Great War](./World_War_I "World War I") was fought on the continent and with the [February Revolution](./February_Revolution "February Revolution") in Russia, the beginning of the [Russian Revolution](./Russian_Revolution_(1917) "Russian Revolution (1917)") also affected Östersund. Rationing led to lack of supplies and a revolution was feared. Some of the citizens, primarily soldiers, went on hunger strikes and at the first of May that year 4,000 demonstrators gathered in front of the city hall demanding lower prices on milk and wood. The year after, the [Spanish flu](./Spanish_flu "Spanish flu") spread the world. The [city doctor](./City_physician "City physician") in Östersund noted that "Östersund ought without objection to have been more haunted by the flu than any other Swedish city", which is why Östersund was referred to by locals as *spanska sjukans huvudstad*, 'capital of the Spanish flu'.[[36]](./Östersund#cite_note-36)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Stora_kyrkan_%C3%96stersund_march_2012.jpg/250px-Stora_kyrkan_%C3%96stersund_march_2012.jpg)](./File:Stora_kyrkan_Östersund_march_2012.jpg)

The large brick church was built in 1940.

Despite the [Great Depression](./Great_Depression "Great Depression") and several crises resulting in a very high unemployment rate, Östersund continued to grow in the [interwar period](./Interwar_period "Interwar period"). In 1918 the Odenslund area was [incorporated](./Municipal_corporation "Municipal corporation"). The business sector remained largely unaffected and Östersund continued to be one of the least industrialized cities in Sweden. Instead Östersund continued to focus on wholesale trade and became a centre for it in northern and north-central Sweden. The city's central position was strengthened when the [Inlandsbanan](./Inlandsbanan "Inlandsbanan") railway was constructed through Jämtland from the north to the south. The first scheduled bus route was created in the 1920s between Östersund and the nearby town of [Brunflo](./Brunflo "Brunflo"). In the next decade well over 40 bus routes were functioning in Östersund. The dairy was located west of the bus square, Gustav III:s torg, at the current site of the shopping mall Kärnan. This square naturally become a central part of the city.

Östersund continued to grow after the [Second World War](./Second_World_War "Second World War"). Lugnvik was incorporated into the city in 1954 and Östersund was, like the rest of Jämtland, affected by the [Rehn-Meidner-model](./Rehn-Meidner-model "Rehn-Meidner-model"), though not in the same way. The Swedish [Keynesian](./Keynesian "Keynesian") policy was launched in order to improve the mobility of the labour force. Jämtland was struck hard by this when the people moved from the countryside to cities, from inland to coast and from the north to the south.[[37]](./Östersund#cite_note-37) As an urban area Östersund was affected by the [Million Programme](./Million_Programme "Million Programme") and urban districts like [Körfältet](./Körfältet?action=edit&redlink=1 "Körfältet") were created.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg/250px-Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg.png)](./File:Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg)

Östersund became the capital of the Republic of Jamtland. Its [flag](./Flag_of_the_Republic_of_Jamtland "Flag of the Republic of Jamtland") can be seen throughout the year at the main town square.

The negative view towards industry changed when the [Social Democrats](./Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party "Swedish Social Democratic Party") came to power for the first time in the city's history in 1952. Industries were enticed to Östersund through the national localization policy and industrial areas were created in Odenskog and Lugnvik. Development was not, as already mentioned, as good in the rest of Jämtland as it was in Östersund and as a counter to the governmental policy, the [Republic of Jamtland](./Republic_of_Jamtland "Republic of Jamtland") was established in 1963.[[38]](./Östersund#cite_note-38) Östersund became the capital of the tongue-in-cheek republic and the home of the freedom festival [Storsjöyran](./Storsjöyran "Storsjöyran").

Östersund continued to grow and in 1970 [Frösö köping](./Frösö_köping?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frösö köping") was made part of Östersund. In 1971 a major reform occurred in Sweden creating large municipalities replacing all the older institutions; the new large municipality was named after the city. As in the rest of Sweden, the public sector greatly expanded at this time. In 1960 the public sector of Sweden constituted about 30 per cent of Sweden's total gross domestic product; by the mid-1980s the number had grown to 65 per cent. At the time jobs were growing in the county council, the government and in the new municipality. The main reasons for the large expansion were the expanded [transfer payment](./Transfer_payment "Transfer payment") to the households that occurred along with growing interest and public consumption.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Everything was financed by heavy tax increases. The entirety of the 1970s was a period of expansion. Besides the new industrial complex the [Frösö bridge](./Frösö_bridge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frösö bridge") was constructed, a new police station, Z-kupolen (burned to the ground in 1989), Storsjöteatern, [Folkets hus](./Folkets_hus "Folkets hus"), neighborhood churches, malls, etc. The county administrative office and the hospital were expanded and large residential areas grew up in the aforementioned Körfältet and Lugnvik areas, as well as in Odensala.

As early as the 1940s, the city tried to have a [humanities](./Humanities "Humanities") [university college](./University_college "University college") located on Frösön. Opposition between cities in Norrland was great and it was Umeå that finally emerged victorious in 1962. Östersund did, however, get a university college for social workers ([socialhögskola](./Socialhögskola?action=edit&redlink=1 "Socialhögskola") [[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialhögskola "sv:Socialhögskola")]) in 1971. Since 2005 Östersund has been one of the main campus sites of the [Mid Sweden University](./Mid_Sweden_University "Mid Sweden University") (Mittuniversitetet). A number of governmental offices have also been built in the city in recent years.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Garrison town
-------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/F4tva%29.JPG/250px-F4tva%29.JPG)](./File:F4tva).JPG)

[Hangar](./Hangar "Hangar") on Frösön

Östersund became a [garrison town](./Garrison "Garrison") when the [Norrland Artillery Regiment](./Norrland_Artillery_Regiment "Norrland Artillery Regiment") (A 4) was founded in the city in 1892, followed by the upgrading of the [Jämtland Ranger Corps](./Jämtland_Ranger_Corps "Jämtland Ranger Corps") to the [Jämtland Ranger Regiment](./Jämtland_Ranger_Corps "Jämtland Ranger Corps") (I 23). This was done with the growing fear of a Russian assault whereas Jämtland-Trøndelag and [Norrbotten](./Norrbotten "Norrbotten") became the most prioritized defense regions. The [dissolution of the union between Sweden and Norway](./Dissolution_of_the_union_between_Norway_and_Sweden_in_1905 "Dissolution of the union between Norway and Sweden in 1905") contributed by enhancing Östersund as a military city and strengthening its presence; the Jämtland Ranger Regiment was located in the city in 1910 and the [Jämtland Wing](./Jämtland_Wing "Jämtland Wing") (F 4) came to Frösön in 1926.

Östersund's importance as a garrison town grew when the city was connected to the [Boden Fortress](./Boden_Fortress "Boden Fortress"), following the construction of the Inlandsbanan railway.

After the fall of the [Iron Curtain](./Iron_Curtain "Iron Curtain"), the destruction of the [Berlin Wall](./Berlin_Wall "Berlin Wall") in 1989 and the [Dissolution of the USSR](./History_of_the_Soviet_Union_(1985–1991)#Dissolution_of_the_USSR "History of the Soviet Union (1985–1991)") in 1991 Sweden had lost its national threat and the demand for a strong defense organization was deemed unnecessary. The issue was debated throughout the 1990s and the final decision came in 2004 where all military presence in Östersund was ended. Upon delivering the message the [Swedish Minister for Defence](./Minister_for_Defence_(Sweden) "Minister for Defence (Sweden)") [Leni Björklund](./Leni_Björklund "Leni Björklund") was publicly [booed](./Booing "Booing") by the city's inhabitants.

The ending of Östersund's status as a garrison town has however created larger enthusiasm regarding the city's future[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] as the [private sector](./Private_sector "Private sector") has grown larger and more companies are being established, much of which is due to the financial compensation offered by the state. The older areas reserved for military activities have been opened up and two more urban districts were made available.

Politics and governance
-----------------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Stadsvapensflagga_framf%C3%B6r_%C3%96stersunds_r%C3%A5dhus.jpg/250px-Stadsvapensflagga_framf%C3%B6r_%C3%96stersunds_r%C3%A5dhus.jpg)](./File:Stadsvapensflagga_framför_Östersunds_rådhus.jpg)

Östersund Municipality is governed from the city hall.



Main article: [Östersund Municipality](./Östersund_Municipality "Östersund Municipality")

Östersund is the capital of Jämtland County and thus, the county governor [Britt Bohlin Ohlsson](./Britt_Bohlin_Ohlsson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Britt Bohlin Ohlsson") resides in the city. Bohlin Ohlsson is the head of [Jämtland County Administrative Board](./County_Administrative_Boards_of_Sweden "County Administrative Boards of Sweden") (*Länsstyrelsen i Jämtlands län*), an administrative entity appointed by the [Swedish Government](./Government_of_Sweden "Government of Sweden").

Östersund is also the seat of [Jämtland County Council](./Jämtland_County_Council?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jämtland County Council") (*Jämtlands läns landsting*). The County Council is the elected assembly of Jämtland County. The County Council's responsibilities lie primarily within the [public health care](./Publicly_funded_health_care "Publicly funded health care") system and transportation between the municipalities.

Östersund is the seat of [Östersund Municipality](./Östersund_Municipality "Östersund Municipality") (*Östersunds kommun*). The legislative body of the municipality is the 67-member municipal assembly (*[kommunfullmäktige](./Kommunfullmäktige "Kommunfullmäktige")*), elected by proportional representation for a four-year term. The assembly appoints the municipality's main governing body, the 15-member executive committee (*kommunstyrelsen*). The executive committee is headed by the Mayor (*kommunstyrelsens ordförande*). Östersund has historically been dominated by [the Conservatives](./Moderate_Party "Moderate Party"), [the freeminded](./Liberalism_and_centrism_in_Sweden "Liberalism and centrism in Sweden") (later on [Liberal People's Party](./Liberal_People's_Party_(Sweden) "Liberal People's Party (Sweden)")) and the [Social Democrats](./Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party "Swedish Social Democratic Party"). Though contrary to Sweden on a national level, Östersund's centre-right parties long remained in majority. The situation changed only in 1952 when the Social Democrats were included and they won an absolute majority in 1962. In 1966 the [agrarian and rural](./Nordic_Agrarian_parties "Nordic Agrarian parties") [Centre Party](./Centre_Party_(Sweden) "Centre Party (Sweden)") entered the scene, along with the minor [Christian Democrat](./Christian_Democrats_(Sweden) "Christian Democrats (Sweden)") and [Communist](./Left_Party_(Sweden) "Left Party (Sweden)") parties. A new centre-right municipal government was appointed and the Centre Party became the largest party in that coalition in 1970. However, since the 1980s the Social Democratic Party has been in power (excluding a term in the 1990s) supported by the communists (now Left Party) and occasionally the [Green Party](./Green_Party_(Sweden) "Green Party (Sweden)") (entered in 1982).
Jens Nilsson from the Social Democratic Party is the mayor of Östersund and has been so since 1997.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Transport
---------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/%C3%85re_%C3%B6stersund_flygplats.jpg/250px-%C3%85re_%C3%B6stersund_flygplats.jpg)](./File:Åre_östersund_flygplats.jpg)

In 2006 [Åre](./Åre "Åre") was included in the airport's name, in order to emphasize its role as a gateway to Sweden's largest ski resort.[[39]](./Östersund#cite_note-39)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6bron.jpg/250px-Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6bron.jpg)](./File:Frösöbron.jpg)

Frösö Bridge

The airport is situated 11 km (7 mi) outside the city centre, on the island of Frösön. [Åre Östersund Airport](./Åre_Östersund_Airport "Åre Östersund Airport") (previously named *Östersunds flygplats*) is an [international airport](./International_airport "International airport") and the ninth biggest in Sweden with roughly 390,000 passengers in 2005. The airport is one of few Swedish airports with incoming foreign charter traffic and the only one with considerable economic growth in that sector.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The [European route E14](./European_route_E14 "European route E14") runs through Östersund from Trondheim to [Sundsvall](./Sundsvall "Sundsvall") and briefly merges with the [European route E45](./European_route_E45 "European route E45") (referred to as [Inlandsvägen](./Inlandsvägen "Inlandsvägen") locally) coming from the north. The two roads are later split in [Brunflo](./Brunflo "Brunflo") where E14 continues heading east and E45 turns south again.

Östersund has passenger rail services to and from, mainly, Sundsvall and Stockholm. [Norrtåg](./Norrtåg "Norrtåg") operates [Mittbanan](./Mittbanan "Mittbanan") from [Storlien](./Storlien "Storlien") to Sundsvall. [Inlandsbanan](./Inlandsbanan "Inlandsbanan") runs in the same directions as European Route 45. Östersund is connected to Stockholm via long distance [SJ 3000](./SJ_3000 "SJ 3000") ([higher-speed trains](./Higher-speed_rail "Higher-speed rail")), [InterCity](./InterCity "InterCity") and night train. There are overnight services to and from [Gothenburg](./Gothenburg "Gothenburg") and, seasonally, [Malmö](./Malmö "Malmö"). Local company Stadsbussarna i Östersund (literally: 'the City Buses in Östersund') has nine routes in the city.

As Östersund is located on the shores of Storsjön, (English: 'the great lake'), it also has a [harbour](./Harbour "Harbour"). There is also a harbour on the Frösö side of the strait. Several bridges span across Storsjön connecting Östersund with communities nearby, [Frösöbron](./Frösöbron?action=edit&redlink=1 "Frösöbron") across Östersundet, [Vallsundsbron](./Vallsundsbron?action=edit&redlink=1 "Vallsundsbron") from Frösön across Vallsundet to *Annersia* 'the other side' and [Rödöbron](./Rödöbron?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rödöbron") from Frösön to Rödön in Krokom Municipality.

Trade and commerce
------------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Ostersund.JPG/250px-Ostersund.JPG)](./File:Ostersund.JPG)

Prästgatan

Like the rest of Jämtland Östersund is heavily dominated by many [small businesses](./Small_business "Small business"). The city is the centre of trade and commerce in Jämtland County and has more than 300 shops. The [retail trade](./Retailing "Retailing")'s [turnover](./Revenue "Revenue") is 30 per cent higher than it ought to be, given the number of inhabitants the city has.[[40]](./Östersund#cite_note-40) Trade in the central business district (*Staden* – 'the city') is mostly concentrated on the shopping and pedestrian street Prästgatan where large local shopping malls such as Kärnan and Mittpunkten along with department stores such as [Åhléns](./Åhléns "Åhléns") are located. There are large clothing companies such as [H&M](./H&M "H&M") and [Lindex](./Lindex "Lindex") and smaller ones like [WESC](./WESC "WESC"), approximately 50 restaurants, shoe stores, sporting goods retailers like Stadium and [Intersport](./Intersport "Intersport"), several supermarkets (Östersund has rather few convenience stores), etc. Storgatan, the street that runs parallel with Prästgatan, is also lined with shops, restaurants and coffeehouses. Unlike Prästgatan this street is not a pedestrian street. Östersund is the city in Sweden with the most square metres of window display per capita.[[41]](./Östersund#cite_note-41) The most prominent figure in Östersund's business life throughout the 20th century was the car salesman (who started out selling horses) [Sven O. Persson](./Sven_O._Persson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sven O. Persson"), founder of [Persson Invest](./Persson_Invest?action=edit&redlink=1 "Persson Invest"), [Byggelit](./Byggelit?action=edit&redlink=1 "Byggelit") and [Bilbolaget](./Bilbolaget?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bilbolaget").[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] A significant real estate owner was [Maths O. Sundqvist](./Maths_O._Sundqvist "Maths O. Sundqvist") (1950–2012).

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Storgatan_i_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Storgatan_i_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Storgatan_i_Östersund.jpg)

Storgatan in late afternoon.

Östersund has had a long history as a [marketplace](./Marketplace "Marketplace") with the already mentioned ancient Gregorie market, tracing its lineage back to the 11th century, held in early March.[[42]](./Östersund#cite_note-42) Despite being banned in 1914, it continued to be held for a couple of years. In 1950, the market was reborn shortly and was completely resurrected in 1986, when the city celebrated its 200th anniversary, and has been held yearly since then.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] In 1948, when the markets were non-existent, visions to restore Östersund's market traditions in a modern version were brought up. The result was the [trade fair](./Trade_fair "Trade fair") [Expo Norr](./Expo_Norr?action=edit&redlink=1 "Expo Norr"), initiated in 1950 in order to strengthen Östersund as a leading centre of trade in the northern parts of Sweden. The trade fair is an annual event just like Gregorie market, though Expo Norr is held during the summer and not during the winter. Expo Norr is usually attended by 30,000 individuals every year.

Like many other county capitals in Sweden the [county council](./Jämtland_County_Council?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jämtland County Council") and the municipality are among the largest employers.

Besides trading and [public services](./Public_services "Public services") Östersund has some larger companies such as [Solectron](./Solectron "Solectron"), [Cybercom](./Cybercom_AB?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cybercom AB"), [Volex](./Volex?action=edit&redlink=1 "Volex"), [Husqvarna AB](./Husqvarna_AB "Husqvarna AB"), [Swedbank](./Swedbank "Swedbank")'s telephone bank and [Telia](./Telia_(company) "Telia (company)").[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Companies such as the dairy cooperation [Milko](./Milko_(Swedish_cooperative) "Milko (Swedish cooperative)") and [Inlandsbanan AB](./Inlandsbanan_AB?action=edit&redlink=1 "Inlandsbanan AB") have located their [corporate headquarters](./Corporate_headquarters "Corporate headquarters") in the city.

A national survey done by the [Confederation of Swedish Enterprise](./Confederation_of_Swedish_Enterprise "Confederation of Swedish Enterprise") shows that out of every company in Östersund Municipality 52 per cent are "very positive towards [globalization](./Globalization "Globalization")", thus ranking Östersund at number eight in Sweden as the most globalization-friendly municipality (2008).[[43]](./Östersund#cite_note-43)

Culture
-------

### Cultural venues

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Thom%C3%A9e.jpg/250px-Thom%C3%A9e.jpg)](./File:Thomée.jpg)

S/S *Thomée* moored in the harbour.

Östersund is the cultural centre of Jämtland County and home to the prize winning museum [Jamtli](./Jamtli "Jamtli"). The museum has both an indoor exhibition area and an outdoor area which contains a number of historical buildings from all over the county, depicting the old lives of peasants, the early city of Östersund and the Scandinavian inland herding. The museum exhibition hosts an interesting set of tapestries, the *[Överhogdal tapestries](./Överhogdal_tapestries "Överhogdal tapestries")*, showing a rich imagery of both Norse and Christian origin from the [Viking Age](./Viking_Age "Viking Age"). The mythical [Storsjöodjuret](./Storsjöodjuret "Storsjöodjuret") (Great Lake Monster) has an exhibit of its own. Another remnant from the Viking Age is [Frösöstenen](./Frösöstenen "Frösöstenen"), one of the world's most northerly rune stones located on Frösön, the island of [Freyr](./Freyr "Freyr").

The county library, Jämtlands läns bibliotek, is located in the city. It is the oldest county library in Sweden, being founded in 1816 by the will of professor [Carl Zetterström](./Carl_Zetterström?action=edit&redlink=1 "Carl Zetterström"). As the library grew it was moved to a bigger facility. The older building is now situated beside the old church in Kyrkparken.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Moose_Zoo_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Moose_Zoo_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Moose_Zoo_Östersund.jpg)

Moose Garden

Lake Storsjön has been trafficked for a long time and the [steamships](./Steamship "Steamship") [S/S Thomée](./S/S_Thomée?action=edit&redlink=1 "S/S Thomée") and [S/S Östersund](./S/S_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 "S/S Östersund") are still in operation every summer. Unlike most boats, they are seen as male and not female. S/S Thomée is the only one that sets sail from Östersund's harbour. S/S Östersund sails from Arvesund, located at Storsjön's western shore but makes visits to Jamtli's steamboat jetty.

[Frösö Zoo](./Frösö_Zoo "Frösö Zoo") was one of Sweden's largest [zoological gardens](./Zoological_garden "Zoological garden") with [exotic animals](./Exotic_animal "Exotic animal"). Prior to its closing in 2019, it had roughly 700 animals[[44]](./Östersund#cite_note-44) including [Siberian tigers](./Siberian_tiger "Siberian tiger"), lions, [polar wolves](./Polar_wolf "Polar wolf"), and monkeys. Frösö Zoo also had a tropical house, a biological museum and an [amusement park](./Amusement_park "Amusement park"). Outside of Östersund in the village of [Orrviken](./Orrviken "Orrviken") there is a moose zoo called [Moose Garden](./Moose_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 "Moose Garden"), allowing close encounters with tame moose.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/F%C3%A4rgfabriken_norr%2C_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-F%C3%A4rgfabriken_norr%2C_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Färgfabriken_norr,_Östersund.jpg)

Färgfabriken Norr

Färgfabriken ('the paint factory') is a centre for experimental culture based in Stockholm that portrays itself as a laboratory of contemporary art. A branch named *Färgfabriken Norr* was established in Östersund between April 2008 and January 2011.[[45]](./Östersund#cite_note-45)

[Gaaltije](./Gaaltije?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gaaltije"), the centre for [South Sami](./South_Sami "South Sami") culture, opened in 1999 and is a living source of knowledge for South Sami culture, history and business.

[Gamla Tingshuset](./Gamla_Tingshuset?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gamla Tingshuset") holds a small cinema, a café, a small venue and practice halls. It is usually a meeting place for the town's youth.

### Events

* The city festival [Storsjöyran](./Storsjöyran "Storsjöyran") (referred to as simply *Yran*, literally meaning: *[The Great Lake](./Storsjön "Storsjön") Giddy Festival*), the oldest city festival in [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia "Scandinavia") and with 55,000 visitors every year the largest in Sweden. Storsjöyran is held in the middle of Östersund the last weekend of July. Although the event starts the weekend before with the opening of Krogstråket when regional bars and restaurants gather near the lake.
* Jamtli Christmas Market is well attended market taking place the second weekend of [Advent](./Advent "Advent").
* [Expo Norr](./Expo_Norr?action=edit&redlink=1 "Expo Norr"), Sweden's oldest merchandise [trade fair](./Trade_fair "Trade fair") held in June with roughly 400 exhibitors.[[46]](./Östersund#cite_note-46)
* Vinterparken ('The Winter Park'), with seasonal lakeside events.

Media
-----

The largest daily newspaper in Östersund is *[Östersunds-Posten](./Östersunds-Posten "Östersunds-Posten")* (ÖP) with a circulation of 30,000 copies[[47]](./Östersund#cite_note-press-47) and the second largest is *[Länstidningen Östersund](./Länstidningen_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 "Länstidningen Östersund")* (LT) with a circulation of 15,000 copies[[47]](./Östersund#cite_note-press-47) (2006 for both). Like most Swedish newspaper they each have a political [editorial page](./Editorial_page "Editorial page"), views of the [Centre Party](./Centre_Party_(Sweden) "Centre Party (Sweden)") are expressed in ÖP and views of the [Swedish Social Democratic Party](./Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party "Swedish Social Democratic Party") are expressed in LT. *Länstidningen* is unique in Sweden, as it is the only Swedish newspaper with [press support](./Press_support "Press support") that has ever made itself non-dependent on state subsidy. [*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Much of the paper's success is ascribed to the then editor-in-chief awarded with the [Grand Journalism Award](./Stora_Journalistpriset "Stora Journalistpriset") (*Stora Journalistpriset*).[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Since 2006 the newspaper has been dependent on state subsidy. The media group [Mittmedia](./Mittmedia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mittmedia") has owned both newspapers since 2005.[[48]](./Östersund#cite_note-48)

Two [free daily newspapers](./Free_daily_newspaper "Free daily newspaper") exist in the city, *[100 procent Östersund](./100_procent_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 "100 procent Östersund")* and *[Lokaltidningen Storsjön](./Lokaltidningen_Storsjön?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lokaltidningen Storsjön")*.

Local radio stations include [Radio Jämtland](./Radio_Jämtland?action=edit&redlink=1 "Radio Jämtland") (a part of [Sveriges Radio](./Sveriges_Radio "Sveriges Radio")), [One FM](./One_FM_(Sweden)?action=edit&redlink=1 "One FM (Sweden)") and [Modern Times Group](./Modern_Times_Group "Modern Times Group")'s [Rix FM](./Rix_FM?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rix FM").
